catalog_quote: Ik must be viewed as a ‘tone language’ because in Ik “the pitch of a word can change the meaning of the word. Not just its nuances, but its core meaning” (Yip 2002:1). ... As a lexical tone language, Ik falls in the company of all the neighboring Surmic languages like Didinga, Eastern Nilotic languages like Teso-Turkana, Western Nilotic languages like Acholi and Lango, and Southern Nilotic languages like Pokot and Kupsabiny. But Ik differs from nearby ‘tonal accent’ languages like East Cushitic Dhaasanac that allow only one high tone per word (Tosco 2001:34). And from within the Kuliak group, Carlin “found no evidence of So being a tone language” but rather that “stress-accent is important in So, not on the paradigmatic level, but rather on the syntagmatic level” (1993:16). ... Unlike pitch or tonal accent languages, Ik exhibits a wide range of lexical tone patterns or ‘melodies’. These…

audit.quote_check: confirmed in the copy we hold
audit.reasoning: The classification 'tonal' (tonal-OR-pitch accent, domain not stated by the source) rests on the best available description: a 747-pp 2014 reference grammar with a full tone chapter, held held by the project, cross-checked against the same author's 2017 LangSci sketch, also. Every fragment of the deciding quotation was re-verified verbatim at the stated printed pages (2014 pp. 99, 100, 103, 124; 2017 p. 489). The grammar explicitly calls Ik a lexical tone language, explicitly distinguishes it from pitch/tonal-accent languages (no limit on H tones per word), contrasts it with stress-accent So, and nowhere states a word-stress rule; the only prosodic hedge (possible syllable-weight/tone interaction, 'rules yet to be discovered') is already captured in the record's domain_quote.
